title: FAA Part 107 airspace practice questions
description: Free FAA Part 107 airspace practice questions on 14 CFR 107.41-107.47 and airspace classes. Every answer is explained and linked to its source.

questions.question: Which airspace does 107.41 list as requiring prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC) before a small unmanned aircraft is operated there?

options.A: Class A and Class G airspace only
options.B: Class B, Class C or Class D airspace, and the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport
options.C: Any airspace above 400 feet AGL, whatever its class
options.D: Federal Airways within Class E airspace only

questions.explanation: 107.41 covers "Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport" and requires "prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC)."

source.title: eCFR: 14 CFR 107.41, Operation in certain airspace (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC).

questions.question: Which Class E airspace does 107.41 cover with its requirement for prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC)?

options.A: All Class E airspace below 1,200 feet AGL
options.B: Only Class E airspace above FL 600
options.C: The airspace within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport
options.D: Every Federal Airway, at any altitude

questions.explanation: 107.41 bars operation in Class B, C or D airspace "or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC)."

source.title: eCFR: 14 CFR 107.41, Operation in certain airspace (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC).

questions.topic: Class E, Class G and the Class A floor
questions.question: According to the Study Guide, what does designating a large amount of the airspace over the United States as Class E airspace provide?

options.A: Airspace reserved for military training routes only
options.B: Airspace in which no ATC service is provided
options.C: Airspace closed to all unmanned aircraft
options.D: Sufficient airspace for the safe control and separation of aircraft during IFR operations

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "A large amount of the airspace over the United States is designated as Class E airspace. This provides sufficient airspace for the safe control and separation of aircraft during IFR operations."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: A large amount of the airspace over the United States is designated as Class E airspace. This provides sufficient airspace for the safe control and separation of aircraft during IFR operations.

questions.question: What does 107.43 prohibit?

options.A: Operating a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base
options.B: Operating a small unmanned aircraft from any airport property
options.C: Operating a small unmanned aircraft while an airport's control tower is closed
options.D: Operating a small unmanned aircraft over any public-use runway

questions.explanation: 107.43: "No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base."

source.title: eCFR: 14 CFR 107.43, Operation in the vicinity of airports (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base.

questions.question: According to the Study Guide, what do the primary airport(s) within a terminal radar service area (TRSA) become?

options.A: Class B airspace
options.B: Class D airspace
options.C: Class G airspace
options.D: A restricted area

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "The primary airport(s) within the TRSA become(s) Class D airspace."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: The primary airport(s) within the TRSA become(s) Class D airspace.

questions.question: Under 107.45, what must a person have to operate a small unmanned aircraft in a prohibited or restricted area?

options.A: A Federal Airways clearance from Flight Service
options.B: Written consent from the nearest landowner
options.C: Permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate
options.D: A NOTAM published by the person

questions.explanation: 107.45 bars operation in prohibited or restricted areas "unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate."

source.title: eCFR: 14 CFR 107.45, Operation in prohibited or restricted areas (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in prohibited or restricted areas unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate.

questions.question: Which provisions does 107.47 require a person acting as remote pilot in command to comply with?

options.A: §§ 91.137 through 91.145 and 99.7 of 14 CFR
options.B: §§ 91.103 and 91.111 of 14 CFR only
options.C: Part 89 of 14 CFR only

questions.explanation: 107.47: "A person acting as a remote pilot in command must comply with the provisions of §§ 91.137 through 91.145 and 99.7 of this chapter."

source.title: eCFR: 14 CFR 107.47, Flight restrictions in the proximity of certain areas designated by notice to airmen (as of Nov 3, 2026)

questions.evidence: A person acting as a remote pilot in command must comply with the provisions of §§ 91.137 through 91.145 and 99.7 of this chapter.

questions.question: What two categories of airspace does the FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide describe?

options.A: Domestic and international
options.B: Visual and instrument
options.C: Civil and military
options.D: Regulatory and nonregulatory

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "The two categories of airspace are: regulatory and nonregulatory."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: The two categories of airspace are: regulatory and nonregulatory.

questions.question: Which four types of airspace does the Study Guide list within the two airspace categories?

options.A: Controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other airspace
options.B: Class A, Class B, Class C and Class D
options.C: Terminal, en route, oceanic and polar
options.D: Low, medium, high and very high altitude

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "there are four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other airspace."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Within these two categories, there are four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other airspace.

questions.topic: Class B, C and D airspace
questions.question: How does the Study Guide describe the configuration of each Class B airspace area?

options.A: A single cylinder with a five nautical mile radius
options.B: A surface area only, with no layers above it
options.C: Individually tailored, consisting of a surface area and two or more layers
options.D: A ring from 1,200 feet AGL to 18,000 feet MSL, with no surface area

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "The configuration of each Class B airspace area is individually tailored, consists of a surface area and two or more layers" and is designed to contain all published instrument procedures once an aircraft enters the airspace.

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: The configuration of each Class B airspace area is individually tailored, consists of a surface area and two or more layers (some Class B airspace areas resemble upside-down wedding cakes), and is designed to contain all published instrument procedures once an aircraft enters the airspace.

questions.topic: Class B, C and D airspace
questions.question: According to the Study Guide, which airports does Class C airspace generally surround?

options.A: Airports with no control tower and no radar service
options.B: Airports that have an operational control tower, are serviced by a radar approach control, and have a certain number of IFR operations or passenger enplanements
options.C: Airports served only by a UNICOM station
options.D: Airports with no radar approach control, whatever their traffic

questions.explanation: The Study Guide says Class C airspace surrounds "those airports that have an operational control tower, are serviced by a radar approach control, and have a certain number of instrument flight rules (IFR) operations or passenger enplanements."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Class C airspace is generally airspace from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation (charted in MSL) surrounding those airports that have an operational control tower, are serviced by a radar approach control, and have a certain number of instrument flight rules (IFR) operations or passenger enplanements.

questions.topic: Class B, C and D airspace
questions.question: According to the Study Guide, what may arrival extensions for instrument approach procedures (IAPs) be?

options.A: Class D or Class E airspace
options.B: Class A airspace
options.C: Prohibited areas
options.D: Class B airspace only

questions.explanation: The Study Guide, describing Class D airspace: "Arrival extensions for instrument approach procedures (IAPs) may be Class D or Class E airspace."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Arrival extensions for instrument approach procedures (IAPs) may be Class D or Class E airspace.

questions.topic: Class B, C and D airspace
questions.question: According to the Study Guide, how does the outer circle that a Class C area usually has extend?

options.A: With a three NM radius, from the surface to 1,200 feet AGL
options.B: With a 30 NM radius, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL
options.C: With a five NM radius, from 700 feet AGL to 18,000 feet MSL
options.D: With a ten NM radius, from 1,200 feet to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation

questions.explanation: The Study Guide says a Class C area usually has "an outer circle with a ten NM radius that extends from 1,200 feet to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Although the configuration of each Class C area is individually tailored, the airspace usually consists of a surface area with a five nautical mile (NM) radius, an outer circle with a ten NM radius that extends from 1,200 feet to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation.

questions.topic: Class E, Class G and the Class A floor
questions.question: Which locations of Class E airspace does the Study Guide say sectional and other charts depict?

options.A: Only Class E airspace that begins at the surface
options.B: None; Class E airspace is described only in the AIM
options.C: All locations of Class E airspace with bases below 14,500 feet MSL
options.D: Only Class E airspace above FL 600

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "Sectional and other charts depict all locations of Class E airspace with bases below 14,500 feet MSL."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Sectional and other charts depict all locations of Class E airspace with bases below 14,500 feet MSL.

questions.topic: Class E, Class G and the Class A floor
questions.question: How does the Study Guide define Class G airspace?

options.A: The airspace above FL 600
options.B: The portion of the airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E
options.C: The controlled airspace not classified as Class A, B, C, or D
options.D: The airspace within 5 NM of an airport without a control tower

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "Uncontrolled airspace or Class G airspace is the portion of the airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Uncontrolled airspace or Class G airspace is the portion of the airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E.

questions.question: According to the Study Guide, how is a prohibited area charted?

options.A: As an "R" followed by a number
options.B: As a "P" followed by a number (e.g., P-40)
options.C: As a "W" followed by a number
options.D: By name only, without a number

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "The area is charted as a "P" followed by a number (e.g., P-40)."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: The area is charted as a "P" followed by a number (e.g., P-40).

questions.question: According to the Study Guide, how does a warning area differ from a restricted area?

options.A: A warning area is located only over land
options.B: A warning area is charted with the letter P followed by a number
options.C: Flight of aircraft within a warning area is wholly prohibited
options.D: The United States government does not have sole jurisdiction over the airspace

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "Warning areas are similar in nature to restricted areas; however, the United States government does not have sole jurisdiction over the airspace."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: Warning areas are similar in nature to restricted areas; however, the United States government does not have sole jurisdiction over the airspace.

questions.question: What does the Study Guide name as the difference between controlled firing areas (CFAs) and other special use airspace?

options.A: CFAs are always charted with a "C" followed by a number
options.B: CFAs are closed to all aircraft at all times
options.C: Activities must be suspended when a spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout position indicates an aircraft might be approaching the area
options.D: CFAs exist only over international waters

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "The difference between CFAs and other special use airspace is that activities must be suspended when a spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout position indicates an aircraft might be approaching the area."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: The difference between CFAs and other special use airspace is that activities must be suspended when a spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout position indicates an aircraft might be approaching the area.

questions.question: According to the Study Guide, what is issued to designate a temporary flight restriction (TFR)?

options.A: A flight data center (FDC) Notice to Airmen (NOTAM)
options.B: A sectional chart revision
options.C: A pilot report (PIREP)
options.D: An entry in the Chart Supplement U.S.

questions.explanation: The Study Guide: "A flight data center (FDC) Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) is issued to designate a TFR."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: A flight data center (FDC) Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) is issued to designate a TFR.

questions.question: According to the Study Guide, where and for what speeds are military training routes (MTRs) usually established?

options.A: Below 1,500 feet AGL, for speeds under 100 knots
options.B: Above 18,000 feet MSL, for speeds in excess of 500 knots
options.C: Below 400 feet AGL, for speeds in excess of 87 knots
options.D: Below 10,000 feet MSL, for operations at speeds in excess of 250 knots

questions.explanation: The Study Guide says MTRs "are usually established below 10,000 feet MSL for operations at speeds in excess of 250 knots."

source.title: FAA-G-8082-22, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (August 2016)

questions.evidence: These routes are usually established below 10,000 feet MSL for operations at speeds in excess of 250 knots.
